text: Why must a local variable captured by a lambda be effectively final?
choices: Mutable capture would require the lambda to be synchronized, which Java forbids by default.
The lambda can outlive the method's stack frame, so the value is copied — and allowing assignment would make the copy silently disagree with the original.
The compiler cannot infer a lambda's parameter types if any captured variable is mutable.
The JVM stores captured variables in a read-only region of the constant pool.
explanation: A local lives in Chapter 12's stack frame, and the frame is destroyed when the method returns. A lambda stored in a field, handed to a thread, or returned outlives it, so the value must be copied in. Once it is a copy, permitting assignment would be a lie. JavaScript captures the variable itself, which is why closures over a loop counter used to all see the final value — a trap Java's restriction has no equivalent of.
